paragraphs: Dr. Ashton—Thomas Ashton, Doctor of Divinity—sat in his study in a dressing gown, with a silk cap on his shaved head. For the moment, his wig rested on its stand on a side table. He was about fifty-five, powerfully built, with a ruddy complexion, an angry eye, and a long upper lip. At the moment I picture him, his face and eye were lit by the level rays of the afternoon sun, shining through a tall sash window that faced west. The room was also tall, lined with bookcases, with wooden panelling wherever the wall showed between them. The table near the doctor’s elbow was covered with a green cloth. On it stood what he would have called a silver standish—a tray holding inkstands—along with quill pens, a calfskin-bound book or two, some papers, a long-stemmed clay pipe and a brass tobacco box, a flask wrapped in plaited straw, and a liqueur glass. The year was 1730, the month December, and the time a little after three in the afternoon.

These lines describe almost everything a casual observer would have noticed on looking into the room. What did Dr. Ashton see when he looked out from his leather armchair? From there he could see little more than the tops of his garden’s shrubs and fruit trees, but almost the entire western stretch of its red brick wall was visible. In its centre stood a double gate of rather elaborate iron scrollwork, through which he could see something of the view beyond. The ground sloped away almost immediately into a hollow, along which a stream must run, then rose steeply on the other side to a field resembling parkland. Oaks stood thickly across it, now, of course, leafless. They were not so close together that he could not glimpse the sky and horizon between their trunks. The sky was golden now, and the horizon—which seemed to be distant woods—was purple.
But after contemplating this view for many minutes, all Dr. Ashton could find to say was, “Abominable!”

Immediately afterwards, a listener would have heard footsteps coming rather hurriedly towards the study. Their echo would have told him that they were crossing a much larger room. As the door opened, Dr. Ashton turned in his chair and looked expectantly towards it. A lady came in—a stout lady wearing the clothes of the time. Though I have made some attempt to describe the doctor’s clothing, I will not attempt his wife’s, for it was Mrs. Ashton who had entered. She looked anxious, even deeply distressed. Putting her head close to his, she spoke in a voice so troubled that it was almost a whisper. “He’s in a very bad state, love. Worse, I’m afraid.” “Tut, tut, is he really?” He leaned back and looked into her face. She nodded. At that moment, two solemn bells, high up and not far away, rang out the half-hour. Mrs. Ashton started. “Oh, do you think you can order the minster clock not to chime tonight? It’s just above his room and will keep him awake. Sleep is his only chance, that’s certain.” “Well, certainly, if there were a need—a real need—it could be done. But not for any trivial reason. Now, this Frank: do you assure me that his recovery depends on it?” Dr. Ashton’s voice was loud and rather hard. “I truly believe it does,” said his wife. “Then, if it must be, tell Molly to run across to Simpkins and say, on my authority, that he is to stop the clock’s chimes at sunset. And—yes—after that, she is to tell Lord Saul that I wish to see him here shortly.” Mrs. Ashton hurried away.
Before another visitor enters, we had better explain the situation.

Among his other church appointments, Dr. Ashton held a prebendary’s post at the wealthy collegiate church of Whitminster. Though not a cathedral, this was one of the foundations that had survived the Dissolution and the Reformation. It kept its organisation and endowments for a hundred years after the period I am describing. The great church, the houses of the dean and the two prebendaries, the choir and everything belonging to it, were all intact and functioning. A dean who had flourished shortly after 1500 had been a great builder. He had erected a spacious red brick quadrangle beside the church to house its officials. Some of these people were no longer needed. Their offices had dwindled into mere titles, held by clergymen or lawyers in the town and surrounding area. So the houses intended for eight or ten people were now shared by three: the dean and the two prebendaries. Dr. Ashton’s house included what had once been the common sitting room and dining hall of the whole community. It occupied an entire side of the courtyard. At one end was a private door into the minster; the other end, as we have seen, looked out over the countryside.

So much for the house. As for its inhabitants, Dr. Ashton was wealthy and childless. He had adopted—or rather, had undertaken to bring up—the orphaned son of his wife’s sister. The boy’s name was Frank Sydall, and he had been in the house for many months. Then, one day, a letter arrived from an Irish peer, the Earl of Kildonan, who had known Dr. Ashton at college. He asked whether the doctor would consider taking the Earl’s heir, Viscount Saul, into his household and acting as a kind of tutor to him. Lord Kildonan was shortly to take up a post at the embassy in Lisbon, and the boy was unfit for the voyage. “Not that he is sickly,” the Earl wrote, “though you will find him strange in his behaviour—or so I have thought lately. To confirm it, only today his old nurse came specially to tell me he was possessed. But let that pass. I’m sure you can find a spell to put everything right. Your arm was strong enough in the old days, and I give you full authority to use it as you see fit. The truth is, he has no boys here of his own age or standing to spend time with, and he takes to moping about our ancient earth forts and graveyards. He brings home fantastic tales that frighten my servants out of their wits. So you and your lady have been warned.” Perhaps with half an eye on the possibility of an Irish bishopric, which another sentence in the Earl’s letter seemed to hint at, Dr. Ashton agreed to take charge of Viscount Saul and the two hundred guineas a year that were to come with him.

And so he came, one night in September. After getting out of the carriage that brought him, he first spoke to the carriage’s mounted driver, gave him some money, and patted his horse’s neck. Whether or not he made some movement that frightened it, there was very nearly a nasty accident. The horse shied violently, and the unprepared rider was thrown. He lost his payment too, as he discovered afterwards. The carriage scraped some of its paint off on the gateposts, and a wheel ran over the foot of the man unloading the luggage. When Lord Saul came up the steps into the light of the porch lamp to be greeted by Dr. Ashton, he proved to be a thin youth of perhaps sixteen, with straight black hair and the pale colouring common to that appearance. He took the accident and commotion calmly enough and showed proper concern for those who had been, or might have been, hurt. His voice was smooth and pleasant and, curiously, had no trace of an Irish accent.

Frank Sydall was younger, perhaps eleven or twelve, but Lord Saul did not reject his company for that. Frank could teach him various games he had not known in Ireland, and he learned them readily. He was quick at his books too, although he had had little or no regular teaching at home. Before long, he was managing to puzzle out the inscriptions on the minster’s tombs. He often asked the doctor questions about the library’s old books that required some thought to answer. We must suppose that he made himself very agreeable to the servants, for within ten days they were almost falling over one another in their efforts to please him. At the same time, Mrs. Ashton was having some difficulty finding new maidservants. There were several changes, and some of the town families that had usually supplied them seemed to have no one available. She was forced to look further afield than usual.

I gather these general details from the doctor’s diary notes and letters. They are generalities, and in view of what must be told, we would like something clearer and more detailed. We find it in entries beginning late in the year. I think they were all written up together after the final incident. But they cover so few days altogether that there is no reason to doubt the writer’s ability to remember the sequence of events accurately.

On a Friday morning, a fox—or perhaps a cat—carried off Mrs. Ashton’s most treasured black cockerel, a bird without a single white feather. Her husband had often told her that it would make a suitable sacrifice to Æsculapius. This had greatly upset her, and now she could hardly be comforted. The boys searched everywhere for traces of the bird. Lord Saul brought in a few feathers that seemed to have been partly burnt on the garden rubbish heap. That same day, Dr. Ashton looked out of an upstairs window and saw the boys playing a game he did not understand in a corner of the garden. Frank was staring intently at something in his palm. Saul stood behind him and seemed to be listening. After several minutes, he laid his hand very gently on Frank’s head. Almost at once, Frank dropped whatever he was holding, pressed his hands over his eyes, and sank onto the grass. With great anger on his face, Saul hastily picked up the object. All that could be seen of it was that it glittered. He put it in his pocket and turned away, leaving Frank huddled on the grass. Dr. Ashton tapped on the window to attract their attention. Saul looked up, apparently alarmed, then sprang towards Frank, pulled him up by the arm, and led him away. When they came in to dinner, Saul explained that they had been acting part of the tragedy Radamistus. In it, the heroine reads the future of her father’s kingdom in a glass ball held in her hand and is overwhelmed by the terrible events she sees. Frank said nothing during this explanation, but looked at Saul rather bewilderedly. Mrs. Ashton thought he must have caught a chill from the wet grass. That evening, he was certainly feverish and unwell. His mind was troubled as well as his body, for he seemed to have something he wanted to tell her. But a rush of household business prevented her from listening to him. Later, she went to the boys’ bedroom, as usual, to make sure their light had been taken away and to wish them goodnight. Frank seemed to be asleep, though she thought his face looked unnaturally flushed. Lord Saul, however, was pale and quiet, smiling in his sleep.

The next morning, Dr. Ashton happened to be busy with church matters and other business, and could not give the boys their lessons. Instead, he set them written work to bring to him. Three times, if not more, Frank knocked on the study door. Each time, the doctor happened to be occupied with a visitor and sent the boy away rather roughly, as he later regretted. Two clergymen came to dinner that day. Both were fathers, and both remarked that the boy seemed to be coming down with a fever. They were only too close to the truth. It would have been better to put him to bed immediately. A couple of hours later that afternoon, he ran into the house crying out in a truly terrifying way. Rushing to Mrs. Ashton, he clung to her, begged her to protect him, and repeated without stopping, “Keep them off! Keep them off!” It was now clear that some illness had taken a firm hold of him. He was put to bed in a different room from his usual one, and a physician was brought to see him. The physician declared that the illness was serious and affected the boy’s brain. He predicted that it would be fatal unless the boy was kept absolutely quiet and given the sedatives he would prescribe.
By another route, we have now reached the point where we were before. The minster clock has been stopped from striking, and Lord Saul stands on the study’s threshold.

“What can you tell me about this poor boy’s condition?” was Dr. Ashton’s first question. “Why, sir, little more than you already know, I imagine. I must blame myself, though, for frightening him yesterday when we were acting that foolish play you saw. I fear I made him take it more to heart than I intended.” “How so?” “Well, by telling him foolish stories I had picked up in Ireland about what we call second sight.” “Second sight! What kind of sight is that?” “Well, you know our ignorant people claim that some can foresee what is to come—sometimes in a glass, or in the air, perhaps. At Kildonan we had an old woman who claimed that power. I daresay I made the story more vivid than I should have, but I never dreamed Frank would take it as much to heart as he did.” “You were wrong, my lord, very wrong, to meddle with such superstitions at all. You should have considered whose house you were in, and how unbecoming such behaviour is to my position and character, or to your own. But tell me: while acting a play, as you say, how did you come upon anything that could frighten Frank so badly?” “That is what I can hardly explain, sir. In an instant, he went from ranting about battles and lovers and Cleodora and Antigenes to something I could not follow at all. Then he fell down, as you saw.” “Yes. Was that when you put your hand on top of his head?” Lord Saul shot his questioner a quick, spiteful look. For the first time, he did not seem ready with an answer. “It may have been about then,” he said. “I have tried to remember, but I am not sure. At any rate, there was no significance in what I did.” “Ah!” said Dr. Ashton. “Well, my lord, I would be failing in my duty if I did not tell you that this fright may have very serious consequences for my poor nephew. The physician speaks very gloomily about his condition.” Lord Saul pressed his hands together and looked earnestly at Dr. Ashton. “I am willing to believe that you had no bad intentions, since you could certainly have no reason to bear the poor boy any malice. But I cannot consider you wholly blameless in this.” As he spoke, the hurrying footsteps sounded again. Mrs. Ashton came quickly into the room, carrying a candle, for evening had now fallen. She was greatly agitated. “Oh, come!” she cried. “Come at once. I am sure he is dying.” “Dying? Frank? Is it possible? Already?” With some such incoherent words, the doctor snatched a prayer book from the table and ran out after his wife. Lord Saul remained where he was for a moment. Molly, the maid, saw him bend over and put both hands to his face. As she said afterwards, she would swear with her last breath that he was trying to hold back a fit of laughter. Then he went out quietly, following the others.

Sadly, Mrs. Ashton’s prediction was right. I have no wish to imagine the last scene in detail. What Dr. Ashton records is important to the story, or may be taken as such. They asked Frank whether he would like to see his companion, Lord Saul, once more. In these final moments, the boy appears to have been quite clear-headed. “No,” he said. “I don’t want to see him. But you should tell him I am afraid he will be very cold.” “What do you mean, my dear?” Mrs. Ashton asked. “Only that,” said Frank. “But tell him as well that I am free of them now, and he should take care. And I am sorry about your black cockerel, Aunt Ashton. But he said we had to use it that way if we were to see everything that could be seen.”

A few minutes later, he was dead. Both the Ashtons grieved, naturally his aunt most of all. But the doctor, though not an emotional man, was touched by the sadness of so early a death. Besides, he was increasingly suspicious that Saul had not told him everything, and that something here lay outside his usual experience. On leaving the room where Frank had died, he walked across the residence’s quadrangle to the sexton’s house. The greatest of the minster bells must toll for the death, a grave must be dug in the churchyard, and there was no longer any need to silence the clock’s chimes. As he walked slowly back in the dark, he thought he must see Lord Saul again. That matter of the black cockerel, however trivial it might seem, would have to be cleared up. It might merely have been the sick boy’s fancy. But if not, had he not read about a witch trial in which some grim little sacrificial ceremony had played a part? Yes, he must see Saul.

I am guessing at these thoughts of his rather than finding written evidence for them. There was certainly another interview. It is equally certain that Saul would—or, as he said, could—throw no light on Frank’s words, although the message, or some part of it, appeared to affect him horribly. But no detailed record of their conversation survives. It is only said that Saul sat in the study all that evening. When he finally said goodnight, which he did very reluctantly, he asked for the doctor’s prayers.

January was almost over when Lord Kildonan, at the embassy in Lisbon, received a letter that, for once, deeply disturbed that vain man and neglectful father. Saul was dead. The scene at Frank’s burial had been very distressing. The day was terribly dark and windy. The bearers staggered blindly beneath the flapping black cloth over the coffin. On emerging from the minster porch, they struggled to reach the grave. Mrs. Ashton was in her room; women did not then attend their relatives’ funerals. Saul was there, however, wrapped in the mourning cloak of the period. His face was as white and fixed as a dead person’s, except when, three or four times as people noticed, he suddenly turned his head to the left and looked over his shoulder. Then it came alive with a terrible expression of fear, as though he were listening. No one saw him leave, and no one could find him that evening. All night, the gale battered the church’s high windows, howled across the uplands, and roared through the woods. Searching outside was useless. No shout or cry for help could possibly have been heard. All Dr. Ashton could do was alert the people around the college and the town constables, then sit up waiting for news. This he did. The news came early the next morning, brought by the sexton, whose duty was to open the church for early prayers at seven. He sent the maid rushing upstairs, wild-eyed and with her hair flying, to summon her master. The two men dashed across to the minster’s south door. There they found Lord Saul clinging desperately to the door’s great ring, his head sunk between his shoulders, his stockings in rags, his shoes missing, and his legs torn and bloody.

This was what Lord Kildonan had to be told, and it really concludes the first part of the story. Frank Sydall and Lord Viscount Saul, only child and heir of William, Earl of Kildonan, share a single tomb: a stone altar tomb in Whitminster churchyard.

Dr. Ashton lived for more than thirty further years in his prebendary’s house. I do not know how peacefully, but there was no visible disturbance. His successor preferred a house he already owned in the town and left the senior prebendary’s residence empty. Between them, these two men saw the eighteenth century out and the nineteenth in. Mr. Hindes, who succeeded Ashton, became prebendary at twenty-nine and died at eighty-nine. So it was not until 1823 or 1824 that someone took up the post intending to live in the house. This was Dr. Henry Oldys. Some readers may know him as the author of the row of volumes labelled Oldys’s Works. These occupy a place on the shelves of many a sizeable library that must be honoured, since it is so rarely touched.

Dr. Oldys, his niece, and his servants spent several months moving his furniture and books from his parsonage in Dorsetshire to the Whitminster quadrangle and arranging everything. Eventually, the work was finished. Though unoccupied, the house had always been kept sound and weatherproof. Now it woke up and, like Monte Cristo’s mansion at Auteuil, lived, sang, and bloomed again. On a certain June morning, it looked especially lovely as Dr. Oldys strolled through his garden before breakfast. He gazed over the red roof at the minster tower and its four gold weather vanes, against a very blue sky with very white little clouds.

“Mary,” he said, sitting at the breakfast table and laying something hard and shiny on the cloth, “here’s something the boy found just now. You’ll be cleverer than I am if you can guess what it’s for.” It was a round, perfectly smooth disc, as much as an inch thick, apparently made of clear glass. “It’s rather attractive, at any rate,” Mary said. She was a fair-skinned woman with light hair and large eyes, and something of a devotee of literature. “Yes,” her uncle said. “I thought you’d be pleased with it. I suppose it came from the house. It turned up on the rubbish heap in the corner.” “I’m not sure I do like it after all,” Mary said several minutes later. “Why on earth not, my dear?” “I really don’t know. Perhaps it’s only my imagination.” “Yes, only imagination and romance, of course. What’s that book now—the name of it, I mean—that you had your head in all yesterday?” “The Talisman, Uncle. Oh, how enchanting it would be if this turned out to be a talisman!” “Yes, The Talisman. Ah, well, you’re welcome to it, whatever it is. I must be off to my work. Is everything all right in the house? Does it suit you? Any complaints from the servants’ quarters?” “No, indeed. Nothing could be more charming. The only hint of a complaint, apart from the linen cupboard’s lock, which I told you about, is that Mrs. Maple says she cannot get the sawflies out of that room you pass through at the far end of the hall. By the way, are you sure you like your bedroom? It’s a long way from everyone else, you know.” “Like it? Of course I do. The further from you, my dear, the better. There, don’t feel obliged to beat me. Accept my apologies. But what are sawflies? Will they eat my coats? If not, they can have the room to themselves for all I care. We’re not likely to use it.” “No, of course not. Well, what she calls sawflies are those reddish things like daddy-longlegs, but smaller. There are certainly a great many of them perched around the room. I don’t like them, but I don’t think they do any harm.” “There seem to be several things you don’t like this fine morning,” her uncle said as he closed the door. Miss Oldys remained in her chair, looking at the disc in the palm of her hand. Her smile slowly faded and gave way to curiosity and an almost strained attention. Her thoughts were interrupted by Mrs. Maple’s arrival and her unfailing opening words: “Oh, Miss, could I speak to you for a minute?”

The next source for this story is a letter Miss Oldys had begun a day or two earlier to a friend in Lichfield. It bears some traces of the influence of Miss Anna Seward, that leader of women’s thought in her day, known to some as the Swan of Lichfield.

“My sweetest Emily will be delighted to hear that we—my beloved uncle and I—are at last settled in the house that now calls us master—no, master and mistress—as it has called so many others in centuries past. Here we enjoy a blend of modern elegance and venerable age such as has never before graced either of our lives. Small though the town is, it offers a reflection, pale but real, of the pleasures of refined society. Among the inhabitants of the country houses scattered nearby are some whose polish is renewed every year by contact with the capital’s splendour. There are others whose hearty, homely warmth is sometimes, by way of contrast, just as welcome and cheering. When we tire of our friends’ sitting rooms and drawing rooms, a refuge from verbal contests and the day’s small talk lies close at hand. We find it among the solemn beauties of our ancient minster, whose silvery chimes daily ‘ring to call us to prayer’. In the shaded paths of its peaceful graveyard, with hearts softened and, now and then, with tears in our eyes, we reflect upon the memorials of the young, the beautiful, the old, the wise, and the good.”
Here there is an abrupt break in both the handwriting and the style.

“But my dearest Emily, I can no longer write with the care you deserve and in which we both take pleasure. What I must tell you has nothing to do with what came before. This morning, my uncle brought to breakfast an object found in the garden. It was a glass or crystal disc of this shape”—a small sketch is provided—“which he handed to me. After he left, it remained on the table beside me. For some minutes, I stared at it, I do not know why, until the day’s duties called me away. You will smile in disbelief when I say that I seemed to begin to make out objects and scenes reflected in it that were not in the room with me. But after such an experience, you will not be surprised that I took the first opportunity to shut myself in my room with what I now half believed to be a talisman of great power. I was not disappointed. Emily, I assure you, by the memory dearest to us both, that what I experienced this afternoon goes beyond anything I had previously thought possible. Briefly, this is what I saw as I sat in my bedroom in the full daylight of summer, looking into the crystal depths of that small round disc. First, an unfamiliar scene: an enclosure of rough grass with little mounds, with a grey stone ruin in the middle and a wall of rough stones around it. There stood an old and very ugly woman in a red cloak and ragged skirt, talking to a boy dressed in the fashion of perhaps a hundred years ago. She put something glittering into his hand, and he put something into hers. I saw that it was money, because a single coin fell from her trembling hand into the grass. The scene passed. I should have mentioned, by the way, that I could make out bones, and even a skull, lying untidily on the enclosure’s rough walls. Next, I was looking at two boys. One was the boy from the earlier vision; the other was younger. They were in a walled garden. Despite the different arrangement and the small size of the trees, I could clearly recognise it as the garden I now see from my window. The boys seemed to be engaged in some strange game. Something was smouldering on the ground. The elder boy placed his hands on it, then raised them in what I took to be a gesture of prayer. I saw, and started at the sight, that they were deeply stained with blood. The sky overhead was overcast. The same boy now turned towards the garden wall and beckoned with both raised hands. As he did so, I became aware of moving objects appearing above the wall. I could not tell whether they were heads or other parts of animal or human forms. Instantly, the elder boy turned sharply and seized the arm of the younger, who had been studying whatever lay on the ground all this time. Both hurried away. Then I saw blood on the grass, a little pile of bricks, and what I thought were black feathers scattered about. That scene ended, and the next was so dark that perhaps I missed its full meaning. But what I seemed to see was a figure, first crouching low among trees or bushes lashed by a violent wind, then running very quickly. He kept turning a pale face to look behind him, as though afraid of a pursuer. And indeed, pursuers were close behind him. Their shapes could only be seen dimly. I could only guess at their number—perhaps three or four. I suppose they were, on the whole, more like dogs than anything else. But they certainly were not dogs of any kind we have seen. If I could have shut my eyes against this horror, I would have done so at once, but I was helpless. The last thing I saw was the victim darting beneath an arch and clutching at some object, to which he clung. His pursuers caught up with him, and I seemed to hear the echo of a despairing cry. I may have lost consciousness. Certainly, I felt as though I were waking to daylight after an interval of darkness. That, Emily, is the literal truth of my vision—I can give it no other name—this afternoon. Tell me: have I not been an unwilling witness to some part of a tragedy connected with this very house?”

The letter continues the following day. “Yesterday’s story was not finished when I put down my pen. I told my uncle nothing of my experiences. You know how little room his sturdy common sense would make for them, and how, in his eyes, the proper remedy would be a dose of laxative medicine or a glass of port. After a quiet evening, then—quiet, not sulky—I went up to bed. Imagine my terror when, before I was even in bed, I heard what I can only describe as a distant bellow. I recognised my uncle’s voice, though I had never heard him use it like that before. His bedroom is at the far end of this large house. To reach it, you must cross an old hall some eighty feet long, a tall panelled room, and two unused bedrooms. In the second of these, which was almost unfurnished, I found him in the dark, his candle lying smashed on the floor. As I ran in carrying a light, he clasped me in arms that were trembling for the first time since I had known him. He thanked God and hurried me out of the room. He would say nothing about what had frightened him. ‘Tomorrow, tomorrow,’ was all I could get from him. A bed was hastily made up for him in the room next to mine. I doubt that his night was more restful than mine. I could not fall asleep until the early hours, when the daylight was already strong. Then my dreams were as grim as could be. One in particular imprinted itself on my mind, and I must write it down in the hope of dispelling its effect. I dreamed that I came up to my room weighed down by a dread of something terrible, and approached my chest of drawers with a hesitation and reluctance I could not explain. I opened the top drawer. It held nothing but ribbons and handkerchiefs. Then I opened the second, where there was just as little to alarm me. Then—oh, heavens!—the third and last. There lay a pile of neatly folded linen. As I looked, with curiosity beginning to turn to horror, I noticed movement in it. A pink hand pushed out of the folds and began to grope feebly in the air. I could bear no more. I rushed from the room, slammed the door behind me, and tried with all my strength to lock it. But the key would not turn in the lock. From inside came a rustling and bumping sound, moving closer and closer to the door. Why I did not run downstairs, I do not know. I kept hold of the handle. Mercifully, just as an irresistible force wrenched the door from my hand, I woke up. You may not find this very frightening, but I assure you that I did.

“At breakfast today, my uncle said very little, and I think he was ashamed of having frightened us. Afterwards, however, he asked whether Mr. Spearman was still in town, adding that he thought that young man still had some sense in his head. I think you know, my dear Emily, that I am not inclined to disagree with him there. You also know that I was quite likely to be able to answer his question. So he went to Mr. Spearman, and I have not seen him since. I must send you this strange collection of news now, or it may have to wait for more than one post.”

Readers will not be far wrong if they guess that Miss Mary and Mr. Spearman married not long after that June. Mr. Spearman was a lively young gentleman with a good estate near Whitminster. At about this time, he quite often spent a few days at the King’s Head, supposedly on business. But he must have had some spare time, for his diary is extensive, especially for the days covered by this story. I think it likely that he wrote this episode as fully as he could at Miss Mary’s request.

“Uncle Oldys—how I hope I shall soon have the right to call him that!—came to see me this morning. After a good many brief remarks about unimportant subjects, he said, ‘I wish you would listen to a strange story, Spearman, and keep it to yourself for a little while, until I understand more about it.’ ‘Certainly,’ I said. ‘You can count on me.’ ‘I don’t know what to make of it,’ he said. ‘You know my bedroom. It’s a long way from everyone else’s, and I go through the great hall and two or three other rooms to get to it.’ ‘Is it at the end next to the minster, then?’ I asked. ‘Yes. Well, yesterday morning, my Mary told me that the room just before it was infested with some kind of fly that the housekeeper couldn’t get rid of. That may be the explanation, or it may not. What do you think?’ ‘Well,’ I said, ‘you haven’t yet told me what needs explaining.’ ‘Quite true. I don’t believe I have. But, by the way, what are these sawflies? How big are they?’ I began to wonder whether his mind was going. ‘What I call a sawfly,’ I said very patiently, ‘is a red creature like a daddy-longlegs, but not as big. Perhaps an inch long, perhaps less. Its body is very hard, and to me—’ I was about to say ‘particularly unpleasant’, but he interrupted. ‘Come, come. An inch or less? That won’t do.’ ‘I can only tell you what I know,’ I said. ‘Wouldn’t it be better if you told me, from beginning to end, what has puzzled you? Then perhaps I can give you some sort of opinion.’ He looked at me thoughtfully. ‘Perhaps it would,’ he said. ‘Only today I told Mary that I thought you had some traces of sense in your head.’ I bowed my thanks. ‘The thing is, I feel oddly shy about talking of it. Nothing of the kind has ever happened to me before. Well, at about eleven last night, or later, I took my candle and set off for my room. I had a book in my other hand. I always read for a few minutes before falling asleep. A dangerous habit. I don’t recommend it, but I know how to manage my light and bed curtains. Now then, first, as I stepped out of my study into the great hall next to it and shut the door, my candle went out. I supposed I had shut the door too quickly behind me and made a draught. It annoyed me, because the nearest tinderbox for relighting it was in my bedroom. But I knew the way well enough and went on. Next, my book was struck from my hand in the dark. “Snatched from my hand” would describe the sensation better. It fell to the floor. I picked it up and continued, more annoyed than before and a little startled. But, as you know, the hall has many windows without curtains. On summer nights like these, you can easily see not only where the furniture is but whether anyone or anything is moving. There was no one—nothing of that kind. So I went through the hall and the accounts room next to it, which also has large windows. Then I entered the bedrooms leading to mine. There, the curtains were drawn, and steps here and there made me go more slowly. It was in the second of those rooms that I nearly met my end. The moment I opened its door, I felt something was wrong. I admit I thought twice about whether to turn back and take another route to my room instead of going through that one. Then I felt ashamed of myself and, as people say, thought better of it—though I’m not sure “better” is the word here. To describe exactly what I experienced: as I went in, there was a dry, light rustling all over the room. Then—you remember it was completely dark—something seemed to rush at me. There was, I don’t know how to describe it, a feeling of long, thin arms, or legs, or feelers all around my face and neck and body. They seemed to have very little strength. But, Spearman, I don’t remember ever being more horrified or disgusted in all my life, and it takes something to upset me. I roared as loudly as I could and flung my candle away at random. Knowing I was near the window, I tore at the curtain and somehow let in enough light to see something waving. I knew from its shape that it was an insect’s leg. But, Lord, the size of it! The creature must have been as tall as I am. And now you tell me sawflies are an inch long or less. What do you make of it, Spearman?’

“‘For goodness’ sake, finish the story first,’ I said. ‘I’ve never heard anything like it.’ ‘Oh,’ he said, ‘there’s nothing more to tell. Mary ran in with a light, and there was nothing there. I didn’t tell her what was wrong. I changed my room for last night, and I expect for good.’ ‘Have you searched this strange room?’ I asked. ‘What do you keep in it?’ ‘We don’t use it,’ he answered. ‘There’s an old cupboard there and a little other furniture.’ ‘And inside the cupboard?’ I asked. ‘I don’t know. I’ve never seen it open, but I do know it’s locked.’ ‘Well, I would have it looked into. And, if you have time, I admit I’m rather curious to see the place myself.’ ‘I didn’t quite like to ask, but that’s rather what I hoped you would say. Choose your time, and I’ll take you.’ ‘No time like the present,’ I said at once, for I could see that he would never settle to anything while the matter remained unresolved. He stood up very eagerly and looked at me, I am tempted to think, with marked approval. ‘Come along’ was all he said, however, and he was fairly silent all the way to his house. My Mary—as he calls her in public, and I in private—was summoned, and we went towards the room. The doctor had told her as much as that he had had something of a fright there the previous night, but had not yet revealed its nature. Now, however, he pointed out and very briefly described what had happened along his route. Near the important spot, he stopped and let me go ahead. ‘There’s the room,’ he said. ‘Go in, Spearman, and tell us what you find.’ Whatever I might have felt at midnight, I was certain that midday would keep anything sinister away. I flung the door open with a flourish and stepped inside. It was a well-lit room, with a large window on the right, although I did not think it very airy. The main piece of furniture was the gaunt old dark-wood cupboard. There was also a four-poster bed, just a skeleton of a frame that could hide nothing, and a chest of drawers. On the windowsill and the floor nearby lay the bodies of many hundreds of sawflies, and one sluggish living one, which I killed with some satisfaction. I tried the cupboard door but could not open it. The drawers were locked too. I was aware of a faint rustling somewhere, but could not locate it. When I reported to the others outside, I said nothing about that. I did say that the clear next step was to see what these locked pieces of furniture contained. Uncle Oldys turned to Mary. ‘Mrs. Maple,’ he said. Mary ran off—no one moves like her, I am sure—and soon returned at a more restrained pace with an elderly lady of discreet appearance.

“‘Do you have the keys to these things, Mrs. Maple?’ Uncle Oldys asked. His simple words released a torrent of speech, not violent but plentiful. Had Mrs. Maple stood a little higher in society, she might have served as the model for Miss Bates.

“‘Oh, Doctor, and Miss, and you too, sir,’ she said, acknowledging me with a bow, ‘those keys! Who was it who came when we first took over things in this house? A businessman, that’s who. I gave him his lunch in the small sitting room because we didn’t have everything as we would have liked it in the large one. Chicken, and apple pie, and a glass of Madeira. Dear, dear, you’ll say I’m rambling, Miss Mary. But I only mention it to bring back my memory. And there it comes—Gardner! Just as it did last week with the artichokes and the sermon’s text. Now, every key I got from that Mr. Gardner had its own label. Each and every one opened some door or other in this house, and sometimes two. When I say door, I mean a room’s door, not a cupboard like this. Yes, Miss Mary, I know perfectly well. I’m only making it clear to your uncle, and to you too, sir. But there was a box that this same gentleman put into my care. After he had gone, thinking no harm, I took the liberty of rattling it, knowing it was your uncle’s property. Unless I am very surprisingly mistaken, that box held keys. But which keys, Doctor, is known Elsewhere, because open that box—no, that I would not do.’

“I was surprised that Uncle Oldys stayed so quiet through this speech. I knew Mary was amused, and he had probably learned from experience that interrupting was useless. At any rate, he did not interrupt. At the end, he simply said, ‘Have you got that box to hand, Mrs. Maple? If so, perhaps you could bring it here.’ Mrs. Maple pointed a finger at him, either accusingly or in gloomy triumph. ‘There,’ she said. ‘If I could have picked the very words out of your mouth, Doctor, those would be the ones. Half a dozen times I’ve scolded myself for it—more like fifty. I’ve lain awake in bed. I’ve sat down in my chair, the one you and Miss Mary gave me on the day I’d been in your service twenty years, and nobody could wish for a better one. Yes, Miss Mary, but it’s the truth, and we know very well who would have it otherwise if he could. “All very well,” I say to myself, “but when the doctor calls you to account for that box, what are you going to say?” No, Doctor, if you were some masters I’ve heard of, and I were some servants I could name, I’d have an easy task ahead of me. But, humanly speaking, things being what they are, the only course left is to tell you this. Unless Miss Mary comes to my room to help me remember—and her wits may recover what has slipped beyond mine—you won’t set eyes on that box, small though it is, for many a day to come.’

“‘Why, dear Mrs. Maple, why didn’t you tell me before that you wanted help finding it?’ my Mary said. ‘No, never mind explaining why. Let’s go and look for it at once.’ They hurried away together. I could hear Mrs. Maple beginning an explanation that, I am sure, lasted all the way into the furthest corners of the housekeeper’s quarters. Uncle Oldys and I were left alone. ‘A valuable servant,’ he said, nodding towards the door. ‘Nothing goes wrong under her care. The speeches seldom last more than three minutes.’ ‘How will Miss Oldys make her remember the box?’ I asked.

“‘Mary? Oh, she’ll make her sit down and ask about her aunt’s last illness, or who gave her the china dog on the mantelpiece. Something completely beside the point. Then, as Maple says, one thing brings up another, and the right one comes round sooner than you would think. There! I believe I can hear them coming back already.’

“And so they were. Mrs. Maple hurried ahead of Mary, holding out the box in her hand, her face beaming. ‘What was it,’ she cried as she approached, ‘what did I say before I ever left Dorsetshire to come here? Not that I’m a Dorset woman myself, or had any need to be one. “Store it safely, find it safely.” And there it was, just where I’d put it—what?—two months ago, I daresay.’ She handed it to Uncle Oldys, and we examined it with some interest. For the moment, I stopped paying attention to Mrs. Ann Maple, although I know she went on to explain exactly where the box had been and how Mary had helped refresh her memory.

“It was a rather old box, tied with pink ribbon and sealed. A label pasted to its lid bore the words, in old ink, ‘The Senior Prebendary’s House, Whitminster.’ When opened, it contained two medium-sized keys and a paper. In the same handwriting as the label, the paper read: ‘Keys to the cupboard and chest of drawers in the unused room.’ It also said: ‘I hold the belongings in this cupboard and chest in trust for the noble family of Kildonan, should any surviving member claim them. My successors in this residence are to hold them on the same terms. Having made every inquiry within my power, I believe that this noble family has died out entirely. As is well known, the last Earl was lost at sea, and his only child and heir died in my house. I placed the papers concerning that sad event in this same cupboard on 21 March in the year of our Lord 1753. I further believe that, unless serious discomfort arises, anyone who comes into possession of these keys without belonging to the Kildonan family would be well advised to leave matters as they are. I do not express this opinion without weighty and sufficient reason. I am pleased to have my judgement confirmed by the other members of this college and church who know of the events referred to here. Tho. Ashton, Doctor of Divinity, Senior Prebendary. Will. Blake, Doctor of Divinity, Dean. Hen. Goodman, Bachelor of Divinity, Junior Prebendary.’

“‘Ah!’ said Uncle Oldys. ‘Serious discomfort! So he thought there might be something. I suspect it was that young man,’ he went on, pointing with the key to the line about the ‘only child and heir’. ‘Eh, Mary? The Kildonan family held the title Viscount Saul.’ ‘How do you know that, Uncle?’ Mary asked. ‘Oh, why not? It’s all in Debrett—two little fat books. But I meant the tomb beside the lime-tree walk. He’s there. What’s the story, I wonder? Do you know it, Mrs. Maple? And, by the way, look at your sawflies there by the window.’

“Faced with two subjects at once, Mrs. Maple had some difficulty doing justice to both. No doubt Uncle Oldys had been rash to give her the opportunity. I could only guess that he felt a slight hesitation about using the key in his hand.

“‘Oh, those flies! How bad they’ve been these three or four days, Doctor and Miss, and you too, sir. None of you would guess! And how they came, too! When we first set to work on the room, the shutters were closed, and had been for years and years, I daresay. Not a fly to be seen. Then, with a great deal of trouble, we got the shutter bars down and left it like that for the day. Next day, I sent Susan in with the broom to sweep around. Not two minutes later, out she came into the hall like someone blinded, and we had to beat them off her. I assure you, you couldn’t see the colour of her cap or her hair, and they were all clustered around her eyes too. Fortunately, she isn’t a girl who imagines things. If it had been me, just the tickling of those nasty creatures would have driven me out of my wits. And now there they lie, like so many dead things. Well, they were lively enough on Monday, and now it’s Thursday, isn’t it? No, Friday. You only had to approach the door to hear them pattering against it. Open it, and they would dash at you as though they meant to eat you. I couldn’t help thinking to myself, “If you were bats, where would we be tonight?” And you can’t crush them, not like an ordinary fly. Well, there’s something to be thankful for, if only we could learn from it. And then there’s that tomb, too,’ she said, hurrying to her second subject to avoid any chance of interruption, ‘of those two poor young boys. I say poor, but now I remember, I had tea with Mrs. Simpkins, the sexton’s wife, before you came, Doctor and Miss Mary. That family has been here—what?—a hundred years in that very house, I daresay. They could put a hand on any tomb or grave in the whole yard and tell you the name and age. And his account of that young man—Mr. Simpkins’s account, I mean—well!’ She pressed her lips together and nodded several times. ‘Tell us, Mrs. Maple,’ said Mary. ‘Go on,’ said Uncle Oldys. ‘What about him?’ I asked. ‘Such a thing had never been seen here, not since Queen Mary’s time and the Pope and all,’ Mrs. Maple said. ‘Why, do you know he lived in this very house, he and those with him? And for all I know, in this very room.’ She shifted uneasily on the floor. ‘Who was with him? Do you mean the people of the house?’ Uncle Oldys asked suspiciously. ‘You couldn’t call them people, Doctor, dear me, no,’ she answered. ‘More what he brought with him from Ireland, I believe it was. No, the people in the house were the last to hear of his goings-on. But every family in the town knew how he stayed out at night. And those with him—why, they were the kind that would strip the skin from a child in its grave. “A withered heart makes an ugly, thin ghost,” Mr. Simpkins says. But they turned on him in the end, he says. You can still see the mark on the minster door where they caught him. That’s nothing but the truth: I made him show it to me, and that’s what he said. A lord, he was, with the Bible name of a wicked king, whatever his godfathers could have been thinking.’ ‘Saul was his name,’ said Uncle Oldys. ‘Of course it was Saul, Doctor, and thank you. Now, isn’t King Saul the one we read about raising the dead ghost that was sleeping in its tomb until he disturbed it? And isn’t it strange that this young lord should have such a name, and that Mr. Simpkins’s grandfather should see him from his window on a dark night, going from grave to grave in the churchyard with a candle, and those with him following through the grass at his heels? Then, one night, he came right up to old Mr. Simpkins’s window overlooking the yard and pressed his face against it to see whether anyone in the room could see him. Old Mr. Simpkins had only just time to drop down quietly below the window and hold his breath. He didn’t move until he heard him walking away again, and that rustling in the grass following him as he went. When he looked out in the morning, there were tracks in the grass and a dead man’s bone. Oh, he was certainly a cruel child, but he had to pay in the end, and afterwards.’ ‘Afterwards?’ Uncle Oldys said with a frown. ‘Oh yes, Doctor. Night after night in old Mr. Simpkins’s time, and his son’s—that’s our Mr. Simpkins’s father—and yes, in our own Mr. Simpkins’s time too. Right up against that same window, especially when they’ve lit a fire on a chilly evening. His face pressed to the panes, his hands fluttering out, and his mouth opening and shutting, opening and shutting, for a minute or more. Then he’s gone, off into the dark yard. But they don’t dare open the window at such times, though they could find it in their hearts to pity the poor thing, so pinched with cold and seemingly fading away to nothing as the years pass. Well, indeed, I believe it’s nothing but the truth, what our Mr. Simpkins says on his grandfather’s word: “A withered heart makes an ugly, thin ghost.”’ ‘I daresay,’ Uncle Oldys said suddenly—so suddenly that Mrs. Maple stopped short. ‘Thank you. Come away, all of you.’ ‘But, Uncle,’ said Mary, ‘aren’t you going to open the cupboard after all?’ Uncle Oldys blushed—actually blushed. ‘My dear,’ he said, ‘you are free to call me a coward or praise me as a prudent man, whichever you please. But I am not going to open either that cupboard or that chest of drawers myself, and I am not handing the keys to you or anyone else. Mrs. Maple, would you kindly arrange for a man or two to move that furniture into the attic?’ ‘And when they do, Mrs. Maple,’ said Mary, who seemed to me more relieved than disappointed by her uncle’s decision, though I did not then know why, ‘I have something I want put with the rest. Only quite a small packet.’

“We left that strange room without reluctance, I think. Uncle Oldys’s orders were carried out that same day. And so,” Mr. Spearman concludes, “Whitminster has a Bluebeard’s chamber and, I rather suspect, a jack-in-the-box, waiting for some future occupant of the senior prebendary’s residence.”
